\cpara{The central distinction, wanting to have investigated against wanting to investigate, rests on two borrowed sayings, one misattributed and one I could not trace (see notes). The paragraph asserts a psychological effect of duty (``Consider what happens to you'') and gives no evidence that it happens.}

\cpara{A description of a failure mode with no example and no evidence. It tells the reader what goes on in their mind (``your underlying psychological objective'') and names it twice, as ``motivated stopping'' and ``purchase of rationalist satisfaction.'' Naming is offered in place of showing.}
\cpara{Describes the outcome: you end with a confidence high enough to keep your old plans, but not so high that it looks suspicious.}

\cpara{The contrast case, curiosity, is defined by a feeling (``either direction is equally fine to you'') and by where a curious person looks. No example is given in the post; for one, the reader is sent to an earlier fable.}
\cpara{Contrasts this with the hidden aim of staying on familiar ground so you can finish quickly and keep your old beliefs.}
\cpara{Refers the reader to an earlier fable whose last character shows real curiosity as lightness and eagerness for evidence.}
\cpara{Quotes Le Guin on innocence, and argues that rationalist training risks losing innocent curiosity but should try to keep its eagerness.}
\cpara{Quotes the author's ``Twelve Virtues'': questioning is aimless if you think you already know or do not want to know, and curiosity wants an answer.}

\cpara{The paragraph concedes the essay's problem: curiosity cannot be willed, so a reader who lacks it has only duty. That concession should have been the essay's starting point. It arrives two-thirds of the way through, after five paragraphs describing the failures of duty.}
\cpara{The first remedy: watch for ``sparks of genuine intrigue.''}

\cpara{The essay's one technical claim. It starts correctly (``the expected posterior probability should equal your prior probability'') and then glosses the law wrongly. Conservation of expected evidence says that the probability-weighted average of your possible future beliefs equals your present belief. It does not say that a shift up and a shift down are equally likely, or equally large, or that you cannot know which way the evidence will probably go. A worked case: at 70\%, a test that comes out in your favor 90\% of the time, moving you to 72\%, and against you 10\% of the time, moving you to 52\%, conserves expected evidence exactly: 0.9 × 72 + 0.1 × 52 = 70. You know which way it will probably go: up. The author said as much two months earlier, in ``Conservation of Expected Evidence'' (August 2007): ``If you expect a strong probability of seeing weak evidence in one direction, it must be balanced by a weak expectation of seeing strong evidence in the other direction.'' This post's glosses (``evenly poised,'' ``equal potential,'' as ready to drop to 69\% as rise to 71\%) contradict its own source.}
\cpara{Asks whether, when an argument is not new, you are looking at your belief's strong points instead of its weak ones and repeating old evidence.}

\cpara{``One tiny bite at a time'' sits uneasily with the author's own ``The Importance of Saying Oops,'' which calls ``grudgingly conceding each millimeter of ground'' the error and says it is ``better by far to see it all at once.'' The two can be reconciled (small updates on new evidence are not the same as refusing to admit a known mistake), but the post does not say how.}
\cpara{Introduces a second remedy, the Litany of Tarski, a formula adapted to each case, using the example of wondering whether a box holds a diamond.}
\cpara{Quotes the litany: I want to believe there is a diamond if and only if there is one, and not to cling to beliefs I may not want.}
\cpara{Recommends imagining the advantages of believing the unwelcome answer, and refers to the Litany of Gendlin.}
\cpara{Concludes that any real uncertainty should be protected and grown, since curiosity makes inquiry eager and gives it direction.}
